q: Which NVIDIA component optimizes a trained neural network for inference through layer fusion, precision calibration, and kernel auto-tuning?
explain: TensorRT is the inference optimizer/compiler. Triton serves models; NCCL handles communication; cuDNN provides DL primitives.

q: A team must serve PyTorch, ONNX, and TensorRT models from one server with dynamic batching and HTTP/gRPC endpoints. Which software fits best?
explain: Triton is a multi-framework inference server with dynamic batching and HTTP/gRPC APIs.

q: Which library implements optimized all-reduce, all-gather, and broadcast operations across GPUs and nodes?
explain: NCCL (NVIDIA Collective Communications Library) provides multi-GPU, multi-node collectives over NVLink, PCIe, InfiniBand, and RoCE.

q: Where would an engineer download a GPU-optimized, tested PyTorch container from NVIDIA?
explain: NGC is NVIDIA's catalog of GPU-optimized containers, models, and Helm charts (registry nvcr.io).

q: In a containerized GPU environment, which component must be installed on the host rather than inside each container?
explain: Containers carry CUDA libraries and frameworks; the host provides the kernel driver, exposed to containers by the NVIDIA Container Toolkit.

q: What does NVIDIA NIM provide?
options: Prebuilt inference microservices that package a model, an optimized engine, and a standard API
A cluster provisioning system for bare-metal nodes
explain: NIM microservices are containers with optimized models and industry-standard APIs, part of NVIDIA AI Enterprise.

q: Which offering provides enterprise support, security updates, and a licensed suite of NVIDIA AI software such as NIM, NeMo, RAPIDS, and Triton?
explain: NVIDIA AI Enterprise is the supported, licensed software platform.

q: Which statement best describes inference compared with training?
options: Inference needs forward and backward passes
Inference typically needs more memory per parameter than training
Inference uses only the forward pass and focuses on latency and throughput
explain: Inference runs the forward pass with fixed weights; latency, throughput, and cost per request are the key metrics.

q: Why does training a model need much more GPU memory than running inference on the same model?
options: Training stores gradients, optimizer states, and activations in addition to the weights
Inference loads the model on the CPU
explain: Mixed-precision training with Adam needs roughly 16 bytes per parameter plus activations, versus ~2 bytes per parameter for FP16 inference.

q: A real-time fraud detection system must score each card transaction quickly. Which metric is MOST important?
explain: Online fraud scoring is a latency-sensitive inference workload.

q: Which precision formats are most commonly used to speed up inference on modern NVIDIA GPUs?
explain: Lower precision (FP16/FP8/INT8/FP4) reduces memory and increases throughput, usually with small accuracy loss.

q: In large-scale distributed training, which traffic pattern dominates the cluster network?
options: East-west GPU-to-GPU traffic such as gradient all-reduce
explain: Distributed training synchronizes gradients between GPUs across nodes, which is east-west traffic.

q: Which parallelism strategy splits each layer of a model across GPUs and therefore needs the fastest interconnect, usually NVLink inside a node?
explain: Tensor parallelism communicates inside every layer, so it is kept within the NVLink domain.

q: A 7-billion-parameter model will run inference in FP16. Approximately how much GPU memory do the weights need?
explain: FP16 uses 2 bytes per parameter: 7B x 2 = 14 GB (plus KV cache and runtime overhead).

q: Which statement correctly describes the relationship between AI, ML, and DL?
options: ML is a subset of DL, which is a subset of AI
AI is a subset of ML
DL is a subset of ML, which is a subset of AI
explain: Deep learning is a type of machine learning; machine learning is a type of AI.

q: What is the main difference between classic machine learning and deep learning?
options: Deep learning cannot use labeled data
Classic ML uses neural networks with many layers
Deep learning learns features automatically from raw data, while classic ML usually depends on manual feature engineering
explain: Deep neural networks learn representations; classic ML often relies on engineered features.

q: A model groups customers into segments using purchase data that has no labels. Which type of learning is this?
explain: Clustering without labels is unsupervised learning.

q: An expert system makes decisions with if-then rules written by people. How is it classified?
explain: Rule-based systems are AI but do not learn from data, so they are not ML.

q: Why is deep learning well suited to GPUs?
options: Deep learning uses mostly serial operations
Neural network layers are dominated by highly parallel matrix multiplications
GPUs have larger caches than CPUs
explain: Matrix math is massively parallel and maps well to thousands of GPU cores and Tensor Cores.

q: Large language model pre-training that predicts the next token from unlabeled text is an example of which learning approach?
explain: The labels (next tokens) come from the data itself: self-supervised learning.

q: Which hardware development was the largest enabler of the deep learning breakthrough after 2012?
explain: GPUs made training large neural networks practical (e.g., AlexNet on GPUs).

q: Which 2017 neural network architecture, based on attention, is the foundation of modern large language models?
explain: The Transformer architecture introduced attention-based models that power LLMs.

q: How has cloud computing contributed to AI adoption?
options: It removed the need for GPUs
It made all AI workloads cheaper at any scale
It gave pay-as-you-go access to GPUs without large upfront investment
explain: Cloud lowered the entry barrier by providing on-demand GPU capacity.

q: Which combination of factors best explains the rapid improvement of AI in the last decade?
options: Accelerated computing, large datasets, better algorithms, and an open software ecosystem
explain: These forces reinforce each other.

q: What do AI 'scaling laws' describe?
options: Predictable model quality improvements when compute, data, and model size increase together
Rules for scaling data center floor space
Limits on the number of GPUs per server
explain: Scaling laws show loss decreasing predictably as compute, data, and parameters scale.

q: A retailer wants to show 'customers also bought' product suggestions. Which NVIDIA framework is designed for this?
explain: Merlin is NVIDIA's framework for recommender systems.

q: A contact center needs speech recognition, text-to-speech, and translation. Which NVIDIA SDK fits?
explain: Riva is NVIDIA's speech AI SDK.

q: A city wants AI video analytics for traffic flow and safety from thousands of cameras. Which NVIDIA platform is most relevant?
explain: Metropolis (with DeepStream) targets vision AI and video analytics.

q: A company wants an LLM to answer questions using its internal documents without retraining the model. Which technique should it use?
explain: RAG retrieves relevant documents and adds them to the prompt.

q: Which NVIDIA platform is used to build physically accurate 3D simulations and digital twins of factories?
explain: Omniverse is NVIDIA's platform for 3D simulation and digital twins based on OpenUSD.

q: Which NVIDIA framework is designed for AI-based cybersecurity, such as detecting anomalies in network traffic in real time?
explain: Morpheus is NVIDIA's AI framework for cybersecurity.

q: A hospital wants to use AI for medical image analysis. Which NVIDIA platform is designed for healthcare?
explain: Clara (with MONAI) is NVIDIA's healthcare and medical imaging platform.

q: What is the main difference between NVIDIA DGX and NVIDIA HGX?
options: DGX is a complete NVIDIA-built AI system; HGX is a GPU baseboard platform that OEM partners build servers around
HGX is a cloud service; DGX is a CPU
DGX supports only inference; HGX supports only training
explain: DGX is NVIDIA's full-stack system; HGX is the 8-GPU board (GPUs + NVSwitch) used by OEMs.

q: Which GPU architecture introduced Multi-Instance GPU (MIG) and TF32 Tensor Core support?
explain: The Ampere A100 introduced MIG and TF32.

q: Which GPU architecture introduced the Transformer Engine with FP8 precision?
explain: Hopper (H100) introduced the Transformer Engine with FP8.

q: Which NVIDIA architecture added FP4 precision support in its second-generation Transformer Engine?
explain: Blackwell (B200/GB200) added FP4.

q: What is the NVIDIA Grace CPU?
options: An Arm-based data center CPU designed by NVIDIA
explain: Grace is NVIDIA's Arm-based CPU, combined with GPUs in GH200/GB200 superchips.

q: Which rack-scale system connects 72 Blackwell GPUs and 36 Grace CPUs in one NVLink domain and uses liquid cooling?
explain: GB200 NVL72 is a liquid-cooled rack with 72 GPUs in one NVLink domain.

q: A company needs an energy-efficient, low-profile GPU for large-scale video AI and inference in mainstream servers. Which GPU fits best?
explain: L4 is a low-power (72 W) PCIe GPU for efficient inference and video.

q: Which offering gives access to NVIDIA's AI platform and DGX-class infrastructure hosted in partner public clouds?
explain: DGX Cloud delivers NVIDIA's AI platform as a cloud service.

q: Which NVIDIA platform is designed for embedded AI in robots, drones, and edge devices?
explain: Jetson modules provide embedded edge AI computing.

q: Which NVIDIA cloud service deploys and manages AI applications across many remote edge locations, such as retail stores?
explain: Fleet Command manages edge AI deployments centrally.

q: GPUs are underutilized during image model training because JPEG decoding and augmentation on the CPU are slow. Which NVIDIA library helps?
explain: DALI moves data loading, decoding, and augmentation to the GPU.

q: Which NVIDIA suite accelerates data science and ETL with GPU versions of pandas and scikit-learn APIs?
explain: RAPIDS includes cuDF (DataFrames) and cuML (machine learning).

q: In the AI life cycle, in which stage is TensorRT typically used?
options: Optimization of a trained model before deployment
explain: TensorRT optimizes trained models for inference.

q: What is model drift?
options: A decline in model accuracy because production data changes over time
A change in container image tags
explain: MLOps monitors drift and triggers retraining.

q: Which practice is part of MLOps but NOT normally part of traditional DevOps?
options: Versioning datasets and models and monitoring model accuracy
explain: MLOps adds data/model versioning, model evaluation, and drift monitoring.

q: Which NVIDIA framework is used to build, customize, and fine-tune large language models?
explain: NeMo is NVIDIA's framework for building and customizing generative AI models.

q: Why do teams use containers from NGC across development, training, and deployment?
options: They provide consistent, tested software stacks that run the same way on different GPU systems
They remove the need for GPU drivers
explain: Containers give reproducibility and portability.

q: Which statement best compares CPU and GPU design?
options: CPUs have thousands of simple cores; GPUs have a few complex cores
CPUs are optimized for low-latency serial work; GPUs are optimized for high-throughput parallel work
GPUs are better for all workloads
CPUs use HBM; GPUs use DDR
explain: CPUs: few powerful cores, large caches. GPUs: thousands of simpler cores, high throughput.

q: How many threads are in an NVIDIA GPU warp?
explain: A warp is 32 threads that execute the same instruction (SIMT).

q: Which GPU unit is specialized for matrix multiply-accumulate operations used in deep learning?
explain: Tensor Cores accelerate mixed-precision matrix math.

q: What is the basic building block of an NVIDIA GPU that contains CUDA cores, Tensor Cores, registers, and shared memory?
explain: The SM is the GPU's core processing block.

q: Which memory technology gives data center GPUs much higher memory bandwidth than typical CPU system memory?
explain: HBM stacks provide multiple TB/s of bandwidth (e.g., H100 ~3.35 TB/s, B200 ~8 TB/s).

q: Which workload is a CPU generally better suited for than a GPU?
options: Serial code with complex branching and control logic
explain: Serial, branch-heavy logic benefits from CPU features like branch prediction and large caches.

q: Why do GPUs need fewer large caches per core than CPUs?
options: GPUs store all data in registers
GPUs hide memory latency by switching between many parallel threads
explain: GPU throughput design uses massive multithreading to hide latency.

q: A program is 80% parallel and 20% serial. What is the maximum theoretical speedup with unlimited parallel processors (Amdahl's law)?
explain: Max speedup = 1 / serial fraction = 1 / 0.2 = 5x.
